title: Coping with more wildfires, new risks and stretched services
label: 27 October 2026 · State of the Fire and Rescue Services
summary: Chiefs, the union, local government and the inspectorate told MPs the fire and rescue service is doing excellent work but is under-resourced for the changing risks: more wildfires and extreme weather, new hazards from lithium-ion batteries, an ageing and unsafe building stock, and growing demands on resilience. They want clearer national expectations for the fire role, faster building remediation, national standards and a properly funded plan for surge capacity, equipment, training and staff health.

chapters.title: Wildfires: scenes, strain and a whole-society response
chapters.takeaway: Recent wildfires stretched services nationally and chiefs say dealing with them needs coordinated action, funding and public behaviour changes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Tell us what you saw at this summer’s wildfires and what the Government should do about them.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: The Stourbridge wildfire was the worst I’ve seen in 29 years: widespread devastation in an urban area, heat exhaustion among crews and houses destroyed. Every resource in West Midlands was used while many other fires were burning.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: London also had very high demand: July calls were 40% above the three‑year average, August 49% up, and so far 2026 has seen 20% more wildfires than 2022. We had to recall 2,500 volunteer firefighters and send 300 LFB staff and nearly 60 vehicles to other regions.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: The sector supports a wildfire action plan. But fire and rescue alone can't fix this: local authorities, landowners, national alerts and public behaviour all matter.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Were national emergency alerts useful?

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: Yes. The message worked — we’d have preferred it earlier. It told people what to do during extreme wildfire risk and helped reduce harms.

chapters.title: Equipment, technology and lithium-ion battery fires
chapters.takeaway: Fire services need new kit and national rules for batteries and e-bikes; local services lack capital to buy drones, air support or secure storage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What new equipment or tech do you need?

turns.speaker: Jon Lacey
turns.text: Air assets helped at Suffolk’s Dunwich fire and drones and robotics can assist, but councils lack capital to buy them. National resilience funding should cover surge needs, not force local authorities to reallocate scarce budgets.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: We’ve overhauled training and bought vehicles and PPE for wildfire. Next summer we'll need lightweight multi-purpose PPE and more kit — but that requires funding and local flexibility because needs differ across areas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On lithium batteries and e‑bikes: is regulation and a kitemark needed?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: Yes. E‑bikes and e‑scooters are the new chip‑pan — 20 fires in 2020 rose to 210 in 2025 in London. Many are counterfeit or poorly made. We want the Product Regulation and Metrology Act’s secondary rules to tackle bad imports and the online market.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: They’re a national problem: fatal home fires, recycling‑plant blazes that burn for days. We run a national campaign—“Fast. Fierce. Fatal.”—but science, regulation and safe storage are all needed.

turns.speaker: Jon Lacey
turns.text: Police need safe ways to store confiscated e‑scooters; local fire services can advise on secure compounds away from people, but those facilities are scarce and cost money.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do delivery firms engage with awareness campaigns?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: Yes. Deliveroo, Just Eat and others have engaged with our ChargeSafe sessions — especially rightly where riders use converted or uncertified batteries.

chapters.title: Changing roles: flood, resilience and the Civil Contingencies Act
chapters.takeaway: Fire services are already responding to floods and storms; chiefs want clarity on statutory roles and to be part of a refreshed national resilience framework.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Flooding isn’t a statutory duty for fire in England. How do you handle it?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: We buy multi‑purpose vehicles and train for floods, fires and storms. Summers and winters now both bring extremes — we must plan for both in kit and training.

turns.speaker: Kathryn Billing
turns.text: In rural Cornwall, storms quickly isolate communities. Fire services operate at national, local and community levels simultaneously, so they should be treated as part of the nation's resilience infrastructure, not just responders.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: England has no statutory duty for flooding, Wales does — that’s significant. We want central clarity: tell us what Government expects of firefighters in resilience roles and fund it.

turns.speaker: Jon Lacey
turns.text: We support a refreshed Civil Contingencies Act that clarifies roles and allows fire to step more formally into civil defence, as other European services already do.

chapters.title: Building safety, Grenfell and remediation
chapters.takeaway: Progress has been made since Grenfell, but many unsafe tall buildings remain; witnesses want faster remediation, legal powers to compel owners and more oversight.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ten years on from Grenfell, what progress have we made?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: There’s been progress: new laws, a Building Safety Regulator and better professional standards. But over 2,000 buildings in England remain unremediated and survivors still face injustice.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: In London we still have about 1,600 buildings with a simultaneous evacuation strategy. The Remediation Bill must be faster and provide stronger powers to make building owners fix defects.

turns.speaker: Wendy Maples
turns.text: Councils struggle financially to manage the problem and must be supported; industry should bear more of the remediation cost and there must be robust checks that work is done to the right standard.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would you welcome the draft remediation Bill?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Yes, but push it through quickly and consider giving authorities powers to compel owners and a clear timetable — survivors need certainty.

chapters.title: Funding, governance and national standards
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses say funding must rise, capital needs restoring and a 'college of fire' and national standards should end local inconsistency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Given persistent budget pressure, what can Government do to help services be more efficient?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: We welcome a multi-year settlement, but inflation and rising costs erode value. Fire services lost capital grants after 2013 and must now borrow; unequal council tax flexibility creates unfairness.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: If our revenue had kept pace with inflation since 2011, West Midlands would have about £36m more. That shortfall forces hard choices on crewing and where to place assets.

turns.speaker: Steve Wright
turns.text: Cuts have closed stations and cut crews. We need national standards to stop a postcode lottery in pay, training and equipment; a college of fire could set and enforce those.

turns.speaker: Roy Wilsher
turns.text: Inspection shows many improvements in leadership and protection, but response surge capacity and capital investment remain major weaknesses.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would a college of fire set mandatory standards?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Yes: a college could drive consistent training, competence and professional standards across services — but it needs legislation and funding to work.

chapters.title: People, health and equality at work
chapters.takeaway: Recruitment, on-call fragility, firefighter cancer risks, wellbeing and inclusion all need action: better pay and health monitoring, plus protections for diversity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is staff retention a problem, and do younger recruits stay?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Whole‑time retention is broadly okay, but the on‑call system is fragile: fewer people can be released from day jobs to respond, and that limits coverage.

turns.speaker: Jon Lacey
turns.text: On‑call volunteers do a huge job, but long spells in spate conditions are not sustainable: we need flexible surge solutions and employer/public support to keep them available.

turns.speaker: Steve Wright
turns.text: Firefighters face increased cancer risk from contaminants. Our DECON campaign calls for station investment, national health monitoring (promised for 2027) and consideration of presumptive legislation for work-related cancers.

turns.speaker: Roy Wilsher
turns.text: Our 2023 inspections found cultural and misconduct problems; by 2026 the code of ethics is better embedded and behaviours are improving, but more work remains on diversity and inclusion.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final short point from each: what single action should MPs recommend now?

turns.speaker: Kathryn Billing
turns.text: Recognise the fire service as central to national resilience, give clear expectations and fund capacity now, not after the next crisis.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Smith
turns.text: Fund surge capacity, PPE and training tailored to local risk while backing a national plan for wildfires and building safety remediation.

turns.speaker: Simon Tuhill
turns.text: Give statutory clarity on roles such as flood response and restore capital funding so services can buy modern kit.

turns.speaker: Steve Wright
turns.text: Back a professionalisation agenda with proper funding — a college of fire, health protections, and resources to stop frontline cuts.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Create national standards, get the college of fire established and match funding to the real risk and demand we face.

turns.speaker: Roy Wilsher
turns.text: Ensure inspectorates and sector bodies are involved in planning; resource surge capacity and capital so improvements are sustainable.

turns.speaker: Wendy Maples
turns.text: Ensure democratic oversight and training for local councillors on building safety and resilience, and press industry to pay for remediation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all — we will press the Government on these points and ask for evidence to back reforms on the Civil Contingencies Act, remediation and funding.
